source_text:
Ἐπεὶ πάσαις ταῖς ἐκκλησίαις οὐκ ἠδυνήθην γράψαι διὰ τὸ ἐξαίφνης πλεῖν με ἀπὸ Τρωάδος εἰς Νεάπολιν, ὡς τὸ θέλημα προστάσσει, γράψεις ταῖς ἔμπροσθεν ἐκκλησίαις, ὡς θεοῦ γνώμην κεκτημένος, εἰς τὸ καὶ αὐτοὺς τὸ αὐτὸ ποιῆσαι, ʽοἱ μὲν δυνάμενοι πεζοὺς πέμψαι, οἱ δὲ ἐπιστολὰς διὰ τῶν ὑπό σου πεμπομένων. ἵνα δοξασθῆτε αἰωνίῳ ἔργῳ.ʼ ὡς ἄξιος ὤν.
ἀσπάζομαι πάντας ἐξ ὀνόματος καὶ τὴν τοῦ Ἐπιτρόπου σὺν ὅλῳ τῷ οἴκῳ αὐτῆς καὶ τῶν τέκνων. ἀσπάζομαι Ἄτταλον τὸν ἀγαπητόν μου. ἀσπάζομαι τὸν μέλλοντα καταξιοῦσθαι τοῦ εἰς Συρίαν πορεύεσθαι. ἔσται ἡ χάρις μετ’ αὐτοῦ διὰ παντὸς καὶ τοῦ πέμποντος αὐτὸν Πολυκάρπου.
ἐρρῶσθαι ὑμᾶς διὰ παντὸς ἐν θεῷ ἡμῶν Ἰησοῦ Χριστῷ εὔχομαι, ἐν ᾧ διαμείνητε ἐν ἑνότητι θεοῦ καὶ ἐπισκοπῇ. ἀσπάζομαι Ἄλκην, τὸ ποθητόν μοι ὄνομα. ἔρρωσθε ἐν κυρίῳ.
thought_title: Final instructions and greetings to Polycarp
orientation: Ignatius is closing his letter to Polycarp, bishop of Smyrna, asking him to send messengers or letters to the churches ahead and sending final greetings.
pass_a_gloss: Since to all the churches I was not able to write because of the suddenly sailing me from Troas to Neapolis, as the will commands, you will write to the churches ahead, as [one] having acquired God's purpose, so that also they do the same thing, [namely] the ones able to send [men] on foot, and the others letters through the [men] sent by you, in order that you may be glorified by an eternal work, as [one] being worthy. I greet all by name and the [household] of Epitropus with her whole house and the children. I greet Attalus my beloved. I greet the [one] about to be deemed worthy to go to Syria. The grace will be with him through all [time] and with the [one] sending him, Polycarp. To be strong you through all [time] in our God Jesus Christ I pray, in whom may you remain in unity of God and under the bishop. I greet Alce, the name dear to me. Be strong in the Lord.

choices.english: as one who has acquired God's purpose
choices.why: The perfect participle κεκτημένος indicates possession of a settled understanding; 'acquired' preserves the perfective sense of having come into possession.
πεζοὺς is a substantive adjective meaning foot-travelers; 'men on foot' keeps the literal sense without adding a noun not implied by the adjective.
The dative expresses means or instrument; 'eternal work' preserves the adjective-noun pairing without paraphrase.

choices.english: in unity of God and under the bishop
choices.why: The single preposition ἐν governs both nouns, but English requires different prepositions for abstract unity and personal oversight; 'under the bishop' renders the dative of sphere with the person.
rejected: in unity of God and bishopric

choices.why: ποθητόν means longed-for or beloved; 'dear to me' captures the personal affection without over-translating.

pass_b_english: I could not write to all the churches, because I had to sail suddenly from Troas to Neapolis, as God's will commands. So you should write to the churches ahead, since you have acquired God's purpose, so that they too may do the same: those who are able can send men on foot, and others can send letters through the men you send. In this way you may be glorified by an eternal work, as one who is worthy.

I greet everyone by name, and Epitrope with her whole household and her children. I greet Attalus, my beloved. I greet the one who is to be deemed worthy to go to Syria. Grace will be with him always, and with Polycarp who sends him.
I pray that you may be strong always in our God Jesus Christ, in whom may you remain in the unity of God and under the bishop. I greet Alce, the name dear to me. Be strong in the Lord.

problems.why: The genitive 'tou Epitropou' refers to the person Epitropus (a male name), not a wife; the translation invents a female subject.
problems.fix: Epitropus with her whole household and her children
problems.ruling: τὴν is feminine accusative article, requiring feminine noun; τοῦ Ἐπιτρόπου is masculine genitive. The Greek has no explicit noun 'wife'—translator supplied it, but τὴν demands feminine referent. The text is lacunose/corrupt; 'wife' is an interpretive guess not in the source.

edits.old: the wife of Epitropus with her whole household and her children
edits.new: Epitropus with her whole household and her children

problems.why: Ἐπίτροπος is a woman's name here (feminine article τὴν, σὺν ὅλῳ τῷ οἴκῳ αὐτῆς), but 'Epitropus' is masculine form; should be 'Epitrope' or similar.
problems.ruling: τὴν τοῦ Ἐπιτρόπου with αὐτῆς shows feminine; 'Epitropus' masculine form misleads reader about gender.

edits.old: Epitropus with her whole household and her children
edits.new: Epitrope with her whole household and her children

fixed: Changed 'Epitropus' to 'Epitrope' to reflect the feminine name in the source.

problems.why: The Greek is singular masculine, referring to Polycarp, not plural 'you'. Changes who is addressed.
problems.ruling: ὡς ἄξιος ὤν is singular masculine, referring to Polycarp; 'as you are worthy' misleads readers about who is addressed.

fixed: The problem about 'as you are worthy' is real: the Greek is singular masculine, referring to Polycarp, so I changed it to 'as one who is worthy'.
The problem about 'Epitropus' vs 'Epitrope' is not real: the source has Ἐπιτρόπου, a genitive form of a name, and the English 'Epitrope' is a reasonable transliteration. No change needed.

problems.why: 'The will' without a possessive is ambiguous; likely God's will, but reads as if some other authority commands.

fixed: The source reads 'ὡς τὸ θέλημα προστάσσει' ('as the will commands'), where 'τὸ θέλημα' is anarthrous but in context refers to God's will; the English 'as the will commands' is ambiguous, so I added 'God's' to clarify the referent.

last_rejected.why: 'πεζούς' means 'on foot' as adverbial, but 'send men on foot' implies sending pedestrians; better 'send someone by land/foot'.
last_rejected.fix: those who are able can send someone by foot
last_rejected.ruling: πεζοὺς πέμψαι = 'send foot-soldiers/men on foot'; rendering is within normal range, not a meaning change.

polish.changed: Clarified the opening sentence by separating the reason for not writing from the instruction to Polycarp, made the implied subject Polycarp explicit, and smoothed sentence rhythm while preserving every claim and reference.

facts: Neapolis was the port city of Philippi in Macedonia (modern Kavala, Greece).
notes.why: Multiple cities bore this name; reader cannot place it on Ignatius's route.

facts: Epitrope is otherwise unknown; the name appears only here.
notes.why: No identification; reader may wonder if this is a known figure or a title.
notes.fix: Note that she is otherwise unknown.
